entries.title: The long days
entries.text: At this season the sun is long in the sky and the true dark is short, a quarter of the day or less.

entries.title: The stages of the dark
entries.text: After the sun goes there is a little while of dusk, then a grey while, then the true dark. Before dawn the grey comes back, and that is when they go.
entries.sources: C4 s1 COMPUTED; last clause the game rule (ADAPTED)

entries.title: The waning moon
entries.text: The moon rose later again, and thinner. By the sixth night there will be hours with no moon at all.

entries.title: Taken
entries.text: I was born a Christian in a village of the Balkans. As a boy I was taken for the Sultan's service, made a Muslim, and set to work in a Turkish household's fields before the drill-yard had me.
entries.sources: F1 s1 ATTESTED pipeline; birthplace unnamed (map s6 decision 4 default)

entries.title: The corps
entries.text: I am a janissary of an orta: raised in barracks, forbidden a wife, paid a few times a year. Obedience, order, endurance. That is what I still own.

entries.title: Cut off
entries.text: When the Wallachian's riders came out of the dark for the Sultan's tent, my company was overrun. When the army marched, I was not with it. I did not run. I was left.

entries.title: What a deserter gets
entries.text: In the barracks they said a man who runs from the corps in war is strangled and put in the water by night. Every day I live here I must be able to say how I came to be left.
entries.sources: F1 s1 (popular-web citations: kept as barracks talk, map s5)

entries.title: No one is coming
entries.text: The army does not know I live. Every arrow I loose is the last of its kind until I make another.

entries.title: My kit
entries.text: A composite bow and few arrows, my kılıç, a knife, my mail and dolama, and the white börk that tells any man at fifty paces what I am.

entries.title: The crescent
entries.text: We looked for the new moon at the end of Şaban and did not see it the first evening. It was seen the next. We began the oruç the day after. I have kept the count since.
entries.sources: C5 s0 ESTIMATE: tabular 1 Ramadan 30 May, observed 31 May

entries.title: The crossing
entries.text: Early in the month the army crossed the Danube into the Wallachian's country.
entries.sources: R1 s5 ATTESTED; C5 about 4 June

entries.title: An emptied country
entries.text: We marched through a land emptied before us: the people gone, the herds driven off, the wells fouled. He sent plague-sick men into our camps.
entries.sources: R1 s5 ATTESTED as corrected 5 Sep (emptied, not burned)

entries.title: The night attack
entries.text: Three hours after sunset he came for the Sultan's tent, and the killing went on until near dawn. The moon, past full, rose over the fighting after it had begun.

entries.title: The forest of stakes
entries.text:
Before the city stood a forest of stakes, seventeen stades by seven: some twenty thousand men, women and children. Our own taken men were among them, and Hamza Pasha on the highest.
They say the Sultan looked on it and said a man who does such things is worth much.
entries.sources: R1 s5 ATTESTED; the Sultan's words 'reportedly' (kept as they-say); map s6 decision 9 default (a)

entries.title: The tribute
entries.text: The prince of this country has paid the Sultan no tribute these three years.
entries.sources: H7 s0 (unpaid since 1459); not called the cause of the war

entries.title: Who made the dead
entries.text: Our army made these dead. We do not know how to quiet them. The villagers do, and they have no reason to teach us.

entries.title: Rumour of Radu
entries.text: At the well they say the Sultan leaves a prince of his own behind: Radu, raised at the Sultan's court, and the boyars are going over to him.
entries.sources: R1 s5 ATTESTED; S1 s3.3 keeps him rumour only (signed); not called brother

entries.title: The army leaves
entries.text: The dust goes south. The Sultan's army is marching out of this country, and every straggler on these roads follows it or dies here.
entries.sources: R1 s5, 22 June ATTESTED (the army goes south; it is still in Wallachia at Braila on 29 June, so not 'has left')

entries.title: The village
entries.text: A few timber houses along the stream, a wooden church by the graves on the high ground, and a ditch and fence thrown up since the army came.
entries.sources: village.tmj; G4 PROPOSAL; fence named per map s6 decision 8 default

entries.title: The headman
entries.text: An old man with a hayfork he did not raise. He watches my hands, not my face.

entries.title: Who is left
entries.text: Women, old men and children. Their men went with the Wallachian's host or are dead, and some of their sons died by our army.

entries.title: The woman at the well
entries.text: A woman at the well saw my cap and put herself between me and the rope. She did not speak.

entries.title: The trough
entries.text: She lets me as far as the trough and no further. 'From the trough, not the bucket.'

entries.title: The smith
entries.text: The smith looked at my blade the way a man looks at a snake. He has nothing for me.

entries.title: Broken iron
entries.text: He says our army took his good iron and left him its broken. There is always a bellows to pump, if I want bread.

entries.title: The priest
entries.text: He makes the sign of the cross, not at me but because of me.

entries.title: The gap in the ditch
entries.text: Where the headman stands with his hayfork, at the gap the carts went through.

entries.title: The well
entries.text: The well, and the trough she lets me drink from.

entries.title: The forge
entries.text: The smith's forge, and the bellows he lets me pump for bread.

entries.title: The church
entries.text: The wooden church on the high ground, with their graves beside it.

entries.title: The churchyard
entries.text: Their dead lie on the high ground by the church, the well woman says, under wooden crosses with no names. If the priest grants the rite, a grave dug within sight of his church he will close at first light.
entries.sources: R08; M4.7 Q4a (the built rite radius, placed by the priest)

entries.title: Where I stand
entries.text: They fear me. They have reason.
entries.sources: S1 s8.2 ladder, start below water

entries.title: Water at the well
entries.text: They will let me drink, from the trough, at a distance.

entries.title: Trade at the gate
entries.text: The smith will take my labour for bread and iron.

entries.title: Shelter by night
entries.text: They would let me sleep inside the fence by night now, if I asked the headman.

entries.title: A place at the hearth
entries.text: The priest keeps a place for me at the hearth.

entries.title: As far as they trust
entries.text: He will close my dead the old way, at first light, if I ask it.

entries.title: Not after dark
entries.text: 'Not after dark. Nothing good knocks after dark.' The bar did not move.

entries.title: The gate shut
entries.text: I took their bread at sword-point. The gate is shut to me for good.

entries.title: Seen at the stake
entries.text: They saw me drive the stake. They will not forget it.

entries.title: The Apostles' Fast
entries.text: They tell me they are in a fast named for two of their apostles: no meat, eggs or milk; some days not even oil; fish only at the week's end.
entries.sources: C3 s3.6 COMPUTED; s4.1 GROUNDED; actual observance UNKNOWN (so 'they tell me')

entries.title: The ninth Thursday
entries.text: On the ninth Thursday after their Easter they would not work in the fields. They fear hail on that day.

entries.title: Their Sunday
entries.text: Their Sunday. The priest is at his church. They may eat fish today.
entries.sources: C3; not 'Sunday of the Romanian Saints' (1992)

entries.title: The fairies' season
entries.text: They have just come through the Rusalii, when no one works for fear of the fairies.

entries.title: St John's Eve
entries.text: The girls talk of the night before St John's: yellow flowers woven into wreaths and thrown on roofs, garlic pulled for cures, fairies abroad. It is not a night of the dead.
entries.sources: C3 GROUNDED (Pamfile 1910; Ghinoiu); garlic a cure here, not a ward

entries.title: The strigoi's nights
entries.text: I asked which nights they fear most. St Andrew's eve in winter and St George's eve in spring, they said. Not this week.

entries.title: St Peter's wolves
entries.text: They say the wolves are St Peter's dogs and eat only what the saint gives them. When they howl together they are praying to him.

entries.title: Who is prince now?
entries.text: The army has gone. If the talk at the well is true and Radu stays, the village asks who is prince now, and whom they owe.
entries.sources: H7 P4; Radu rumour only (S1 s3.3)

entries.title: Four in the field
entries.text: Four men lay where I woke. I did not bury them. I did not know yet that in this country the dead do not stay where they fall.

entries.title: A man who was a man
entries.text: Something walked at me out of the dark and I took it for a straggler. It had a dead man's face. It did not stop when I struck it, and it did not run.
entries.sources: M4.7 s7; R1 s1 ATTESTED (the bodily revenant)

entries.title: The strigoi
entries.text: The priest calls them strigoi. He says it is the dead man himself who rises, his own body in the grave, and that he goes home first.
entries.sources: R1 s1 ATTESTED (Murgoci 1926); 'goes home' is the priest's words, not built

entries.title: What the dead won't do
entries.text: Dogs run from the torch. Men run when enough of them fall. The dead do neither.

entries.title: Cut down is not ended
entries.text: I cut one down and turned my back on it. When I looked again it was standing. A struck-down dead man must be staked before he gets up, and he does not wait long.
entries.sources: R2 s3; the window is a [DIAL]; only 'staked' (fire and beheading not built)

entries.title: They lay down at dawn
entries.text: In the first grey before dawn the dead broke off. The ones still standing lay down where they were, as if a word had been given.

entries.title: They go at cockcrow
entries.text: The priest says the dead man's night ends at cockcrow. I have seen it: at the first grey they lie down where they stand.
entries.sources: M11 s2 ATTESTED HIGH; C3 GROUNDED

entries.title: Only on Saturday
entries.text: They say the dead come out every night but Saturday. On Saturday they lie in their graves.
entries.sources: R1 s3 ATTESTED; C3 GROUNDED (Murgoci, Pamfile)

entries.title: The stakes, again
entries.text: They stake a dead man to pin him in the earth. The Wallachian's stakes lifted twenty thousand into the air, with no grave and no rite. If the old women are right, no dead in the world are less at rest.
entries.sources: R1 s2 ATTESTED plus his own thought, not a fact

entries.title: Open ground
entries.text: No one has told me this in so many words, but I have seen it. The bodies left open get up in the night; the staked ones do not. A shallow grave without the priest holds, mostly.
entries.sources: R1 s2 ADAPTED: the game's own rule, never 'the villagers say'

entries.title: Why the dead rise
entries.text: They say these rise: a child born with the caul; one who died before baptism; one who lived wickedly or worked spells; a self-slain man; a body a cat has leapt over, or a shadow fallen across before burial. Even one who would not eat garlic.

entries.title: The forty days
entries.text: They say a soul does not go to its rest until forty days after death. Years later they dig the dead up to see whether the body has gone to earth.

entries.title: The unbaptized dead
entries.text: The old woman says a child who dies before baptism becomes a moroi in its seventh year. I did not ask what her people think of my dead. I think I know.
entries.sources: M11 ATTESTED HIGH; extending it to a Muslim's dead is left unsaid

entries.title: The new moon
entries.text: The old woman says their power is greatest at the new moon, and weakens as the moon grows old.

entries.title: The living ones
entries.text: There are living strigoi too, the old women say, mostly women, whose souls leave their sleeping bodies to steal the milk and the power of cattle.

entries.title: Signs above the grave
entries.text: They say these are the signs of one: a house where they die one after another; the dead man seen at night; church services that do not stop it; a hole by the stone as wide as a serpent; a white horse that will not step over the grave.
entries.sources: R1 s1 ATTESTED (Murgoci's tests); detection verbs are Phase 6

entries.title: The opened grave
entries.text: When they open such a grave, they say, the face is ruddy, it lies turned face-down, and there is blood at the mouth.

entries.title: The moon-eaters
entries.text: When the moon goes red they say the vârcolaci are eating it, and the whole village beats on fire-shovels to drive them off.
entries.sources: R1 s4 ATTESTED; no claim he saw the 12 June eclipse

entries.title: The stake
entries.text: They drive a stake through the heart to pin the dead man in his grave. I have learned to whittle them. There are never enough.

entries.title: Watched while staking
entries.text: The villagers do not like to see it done. One of them watched me stake a man and would not look at me after.

entries.title: The hasty grave
entries.text: A shallow grave dug without rites holds, mostly. The old women have a whole catalogue of precautions because 'mostly' is not enough.

entries.title: At the priest's hearth
entries.text: The priest let me sit at his fire and told me what walks here. I know them now when I see them.

entries.title: The rite promised
entries.text: The priest has said he will come at first light and say the words over the graves I have dug near his church.
entries.sources: M4.7 Q4a; the built wording (map s6 decision 10 default)

entries.title: Burial precautions
entries.text: Where a man is feared, they say, they bury him face-down, with garlic in his mouth, a needle in his heart, or the coffin bound with wild rose.

entries.title: Stories until cockcrow
entries.text: On the worst nights, they say, it is best not to sleep at all, but to tell stories until the cock crows.

entries.title: Feral dogs
entries.text: Dogs whose people are dead or gone. They have learned the taste of the dead and are not afraid of a man. They come in threes and fours at dusk, wherever bodies lie.

entries.title: Wolves
entries.text: Wolves keep off a man as a rule. Here they come deep in the night, drawn from the woods by the dead, and more of them each night.

entries.title: Wild boar
entries.text: A boar alone, or a sow with her young, at the field's edge around dawn and dusk. Cornered, they charge. I set my spear against the rush.

entries.title: Men on the road
entries.text: Not every shape on the road at night is a beast or a dead man. Some are men, with nothing left to lose, and they want what I carry.
entries.sources: S1 s9 opportunists; light-drawn in the build

entries.title: What draws the beasts
entries.text: Every body left in the open calls the dogs and wolves. So do noise and a bright flame. Bury the dead and keep quiet, and there are fewer eyes on the road.

entries.title: Beasts break and run
entries.text: They want to live. Kill one, or show them fire, and the rest may break.

entries.title: Peksimet
entries.text: The last of the army's biscuit. Baked twice, it keeps a year, and it is all the Sultan will feed me now. I have {count:peksimet} left.
entries.sources: E2 s2 GROUNDED; the count ruled 24 Sep

entries.title: What the corps ate
entries.text: In the corps there was bread every day, biscuit, mutton, rice and oil, and pilaf on Fridays. I do not expect to see it again.

entries.title: Hunger
entries.text: An empty belly tires a man sooner. Past that, it starts to eat him.

entries.title: Thirst and the heat
entries.text: In this heat I drink more by day than by night. A thirsty man frightens more easily.

entries.title: The well
entries.text: Water is not sold here. It is let, or it is not.
entries.sources: E1 P2 PROPOSAL; the water rung

entries.title: Village bread
entries.text: Their bread is wheat or barley. An hour at the smith's bellows buys a meal.

entries.title: The torch
entries.text: Pitch and tow on a stick. It throws a small ring of light and makes the dark beyond it blacker. It lasts about an hour. It will not last the night.
entries.sources: E6 GROUNDED; the game's 60 minutes, written 'about an hour'

entries.title: Shield or light
entries.text: One hand for the blade. The other holds the shield or the torch, never both.

entries.title: A flame is a beacon
entries.text: In the corps we showed no more light at night than we needed. A flame on a dark road calls everything that can see it, men most of all.
entries.sources: E6 s4 GROUNDED; opportunists are light-drawn

entries.title: Striking from the dark
entries.text: Strike out of the dark into the light and the advantage is mine. Stand in the glare and it is theirs.

entries.title: A spent torch
entries.text: A burnt-out torch is ash and a stick. One put out early keeps what it had left.

entries.title: The hearth
entries.text: The hearth is the one big light, and a man can sit inside it. It is where the fear leaves him.

entries.title: The sabre
entries.text: My sabre is long and only a little curved, with a plain crossguard. It answers a blow when I am ready for one.

entries.title: The last arrows
entries.text: No one here sells Ottoman arrows. Every one I lose is gone, unless I make more. I have {count:arrows} left.
entries.sources: E3 PRIMARY; E1 P2; the count ruled 24 Sep

entries.title: The mail coat
entries.text: Mail turns a cut well, a thrust less well, and a club hardly at all. Every blow it takes costs it rings.

entries.title: The shield
entries.text: The kalkan turns blows, but it splinters, and no one here can mend it. It leaves me no hand for a torch.

entries.title: The white cap
entries.text: Anyone at fifty paces knows from the white cap what I am.

entries.title: Gathering branches
entries.text: Half an hour bent in the scrub for an armful of branches, and the land near here has few left to give. A man bent over the brush is a man caught.

entries.title: Whittling a stake
entries.text: A branch and my knife make a stake in a third of an hour.

entries.title: Fletching arrows
entries.text: For three arrows: a branch, three goose feathers from the well, three iron heads from the smith, and my knife, three quarters of an hour.
entries.sources: recipes.json fletch-arrows (1 branch, 3 feathers, 3 heads, knife, 45 min)

entries.title: Mending mail
entries.text: With iron wire and a knife I can close the broken rings myself, in an hour, but only so far. A proper mend needs the smith's anvil and a morning.
entries.sources: recipes.json field-mend-mail (1 wire, knife, 60 min, cap 0.75); the time is invented (E3)

entries.title: No coin
entries.text: No one here trades in coin. What they want is work, or iron.

entries.title: What I have to sell
entries.text: I have nothing small to trade. What I have is my back, my blade and a night at the ditch.

entries.title: What a day is worth
entries.text: The Sultan pays me two or three akçe a day. A peasant's day of work is worth one. The Vlachs call the akçe 'aspru'.

entries.title: Weariness
entries.text: A tired man cannot answer a blow. More tired still, he goes into every fight already shaking.

entries.title: Sleep
entries.text: Four hours in the byre by the church wall, boots on.

entries.title: Neglect
entries.text: Go without food or water long enough and the body gives out, no enemy needed.

tasks.title: Stand the watch

open.text: I told the headman I would stand at the ditch until cockcrow.

done.text: I stood the watch. The village counts it.

failed.text: I promised the watch and did not stand it. They count that too.

tasks.sources: map s4; dialogue headman_watch; watch.go dawnWatch

open.text: The ditch fell in where the carts went over it. The headman wants it dug out and the stakes set again.

done.text: I mended the ditch. 'You dig like a man who has dug graves.'

failed.text: The gate is shut to me. Their ditch is theirs to mend now.

open.text: The priest says I should know what walks in these nights.

done.text: I sat at the hearth and heard what walks.

failed.text: The gate is shut to me. The priest will not tell me now.

tasks.title: The rite for my dead

open.text: The village trusts me as far as it ever will. The priest may close my dead the old way, if I ask it of him.

done.text: The priest will close any man I bury within sight of the church, at first light.

failed.text: The gate is shut to me. No priest will close my dead now.

tasks.sources: map s4; dialogue priest_rite; the built wording (s6 decision 10 default)

tasks.title: The Sultan's paper

open.text: I carry the Sultan's paper, taken from a dead man. I must be able to say how I came by it, and how I came to be left.

tasks.sources: R10; F1 s1 ('must not be a deserter'); b4_deserter

done.text: I drew water for the woman at the well before I drank.
I showed the smith how the army forges an edge.

writings.title: The book on the stand
writings.text:
Thick pages, black letters and red. I cannot make one of the letters speak. The priest set his finger on the page and said it without looking down: 'He that dwells in the help of the Highest, shall sojourn under the shelter of the God of heaven... Thou shalt not be afraid of terror by night; nor of the arrow flying by day; nor of the evil thing that walks in darkness; nor of calamity, and the evil spirit at noon-day. A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee.'
He says they read it at midday, at the late office, and over the dead before they go into the ground. I asked whether it keeps the dead down. He said a psalm is not a lock.
writings.sources: Psalm 90:1, 5-7 LXX, Brenton (public domain); uses GROUNDED (modern Orthodox practice); a manuscript on a village lectern INFERENCE; the priest recites, so his literacy stays UNKNOWN (H7)

writings.title: A loose leaf
writings.text:
He read me the verses of the long late office they keep in the fasts, when the whole church answers: God is with us. 'Know, ye Gentiles, and be conquered; hearken ye, even to the extremity of the earth... whatsoever counsel ye shall take, the Lord shall bring it to nought; and whatsoever word ye shall speak, it shall not stand among you: for God is with us.'
I told him that where I come from, the unbelievers are his people. He said that here they are mine. Then he read another line, from earlier in the same office: 'I will both lie down in peace and sleep: for thou, Lord, only hast caused me to dwell securely.' He did not ask whether I believed it. He asked whether I slept.
writings.sources: Isaiah 8:9-10 and Psalm 4:9, Brenton (public domain); both in Great Compline, which is kept in the Apostles' Fast (attack verified); the leaf in a village chest INFERENCE

writings.title: The list of their dead
writings.text:
Two columns, he says: the living on one side, the dead on the other. He reads them before the service, every name. He read me the dead. 'Remember, O Lord, the souls of thy servants: Stanciul. Manea the elder. Tatul, and his wife. Drag.' And on down the page. The last names are in fresher ink and a hurried hand: men who went with the prince's host this spring. Beside some he has made a small mark. 'That one we buried. That one we did not find.' At the foot, no name: 'and those whose names Thou knowest.'
I asked if my four from the field could be on it. He said he would have to think what that would mean, for them and for him.
writings.sources: pomelnic genre ATTESTED (Bistrita 1407, Moldavian, monastic); a village list in 1462 INFERENCE; names COMPOSED from 1439 and 1459 charters; the closing formula COMPOSED; the unanswered question keeps M11 P5 and map decision 10 open

writings.title: The parchment
writings.text:
He would not let me touch it. 'It was read out once, when my father was given it. We keep it for the next prince to see.' The priest read me pieces. 'I, in Christ God the right-believing and Christ-loving Io Vlad, voivode and lord... give to Stanciul and his sons this village, to be their ohaba, and their children's and grandchildren's... And after the death of my lordship, whoever God wills to be prince... let him confirm it. And whoever dares to break it, may the Lord God destroy him here in the body, and in the age to come let his soul have part with Judas and Arius. Written at Târgoviște, in the year six thousand nine hundred and forty-eight.'
'Which Vlad?' I asked. 'The father,' said the headman. Then, lower: 'And which prince confirms it now?'
writings.sources: COMPOSED FROM ATTESTED FORMULAS, not a real document: opening and curse (1439, 1459; press tier), succession clause (Ilie 2023); NO exemptions list (attack: it contradicted 'what they owe'; dues VERIFY); 6948 = 1439/40 COMPUTED (Vlad II); the village free INFERENCE

writings.title: The notched stick
writings.text: A hazel stick as long as my forearm, split down its length. He keeps one half; the prince's man carries the other, and when the two are laid together the notches must meet. There is no writing on it. So many cuts for each house's tenth of the flock, so many for the hay he says they owe the prince, a deeper cut where a debt was paid. 'The prince's man has not come for his half this year,' he said. 'Perhaps no one will.' It is the only book he reads, and he reads it without a priest.
writings.sources: split tally for dues GROUNDED (1708 and c. 1800 evidence); the dues H7 s1 VERIFY; notch meanings INFERENCE (invented); use in 1462 INFERENCE

writings.title: Letters by the icon
writings.text: A painted man holding a book, and beside his head two letters on each side with a mark over them. The priest says it is the Christ's name, shortened as the holy names are written. The old women say that once, inside a church, a holy icon fell on a strigoi and destroyed it. The priest says an icon is not a stone to throw, and that I should stand where I am.
writings.sources: IC XC with titlo GROUNDED; the falling-icon tale M11 ATTESTED MEDIUM (Pamfile 1916), kept as hearsay (no holy hand-grenade); 'barely remember' cut pending map decision 4

writings.title: Cuts in the door-post
writings.text: Small letters cut into the wood of the door-post, some old and softened, one still pale. The priest says men cut there what must not be forgotten: a death, a hailstorm, a year. The pale one is his own. 'In the year six thousand nine hundred and seventy, in the month of June, the Sultan came into the land, and the people went up into the hills with their beasts.' He asked me if that was true. I said it was, and that he had left out the night.
writings.sources: practice ATTESTED for the princely church at Arges, 1352, in plaster; on a wooden village door-post INFERENCE (attack); text COMPOSED; 'went up into the hills' follows G4 and Chalkokondyles and the emptied-not-burned rule; 6970 COMPUTED

writings.title: Graves without names
writings.text: I asked the woman at the well where their dead lie. On the high ground by the church, she said, under wooden crosses, some fallen, and no names on any of them. The dead are known, she says, by who comes to them: on the third day, the ninth, the fortieth, and once a year after. When no one comes any more, the priest still has them on his list. When the list is gone, God has them. I thought of the four in the field, who are on no list anywhere.
writings.sources: no names INFERENCE (inscribed crosses are 16th century on); days 3/9/40 GROUNDED (Byzantine); hearsay voice

writings.title: A comrade's amulet
writings.text:
On the first of the four, a packet of leather no bigger than my thumb, sewn shut, on a cord at his neck. I opened it, God forgive me. A paper folded small, written close in the Arabic letters. I cannot read the Arabic. But I know what is put in these, because every man in the camp knew: the last two of the Book, the refuge verses. So I said those over him: Say, 'I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak, from the evil of what He has created; and from the evil of the night when it cometh on...' And the other: '...from the evil of the whisperer, who slinks off, who whispers into the hearts of men!--from ginns and men!'
I sewed it shut and put it back on him. Whatever it was meant to keep, it did not keep his body.
writings.sources: Qur'an 113:1-3 and 114:4-6, E. H. Palmer 1880 (public domain; 114 completed per the attack); amulets GROUNDED (Met; talismanic shirts); a common soldier's amulet and its contents INFERENCE; the two refuge suras' protective use general knowledge, VERIFY; moved from a dead man on the road to one of Night 1's dead (J2b)

writings.title: The Sultan's mark
writings.text: Folded in oilcloth inside the coat of another of the four: a paper, and at its head the Sultan's mark, tall strokes with loops swept through them. A scribe once told me what it says: Mehmed, son of Murad Khan, ever victorious. The rest is close writing I cannot read. An order, or a pass, carried for some officer who is dead or gone. I know only that a janissary found alone with the Sultan's paper had better be able to say how he came by it. I have put it inside my own coat.
writings.sources: tugra on documents and its wording GROUNDED (dergipark); no claim Mehmed II introduced the motto (attack); the object INFERENCE; carried for an officer (J2b attack: a private letter carries no tugra); dated 866 AH on the paper per C5 -- kept here, since he cannot read it; ties to F1's 'Must Not Be a Deserter'

writings.title: Two coins
writings.text: The smith turned a coin out of a rag to show me what their prince pays with: thin silver, lighter than ours. On one face an eagle on a helmet; on the other a shield cut in two, a moon and a star on one half and bars on the other. He could not read the rim; the priest could: 'Io Vladislav, voivode, lord.' The prince the Wallachian killed, six summers ago. His silver still goes. I showed them one of ours from a dead man's purse. A paymaster once read one for me: on one face the Sultan's name, Mehmed son of Murad Khan; on the other, may his reign be eternal, and where it was struck; and the year, eight hundred and sixty-five. The smith weighed one in each palm and said he would rather have iron.
writings.sources: Vladislav II ducat, legend 'Io Vladislav voievod gospodin', helm-and-eagle / split shield (attack: replaces the disputed Vlad coin, which E1 keeps out); Vladislav II killed by Vlad III 1456 ATTESTED; akce legend and reverse GROUNDED (tertiary), 865 AH; barter framing S1 s8.3

writings.title: Notes in the Gospel
writings.text:
He would not let me near the altar, so he brought it to me: boards, worn leather, a clasp. On the last leaf, writing in two hands. The old one, he read: 'This holy Gospel was given to the church by its donor and his wife, for their souls and their parents' souls, in the days of Io... voivode. Whoever takes it from this church, let him answer for it at the dread Judgment.' Under it, the new hand, his: 'In this year the Sultan's army went by on the road below, and we saw its dust for three days.'
He says books outlive the men who write in them. I asked who he thought would read it. He said: someone who can.
writings.sources: donor notes GROUNDED (15th-century manuscripts; the 1498 Moldavian example); the curse COMPOSED, unverified for colophons; the priest's line COMPOSED; a village Gospel INFERENCE; altar exclusion general Orthodox practice
